I have no doubt it could be obtained, hut perhaps the hon. member would give some further consideration as to just how important it is for him to have it.
The hon. member for York South (Mr. Coekeram) asked as to the number of men serving sentences in Canadian penitentiaries. At the end of October the number was 79.
The hon. member for Lake Centre also asked to have information broken down by provinces, showing the number of prosecutions of N.R.M.A. men for desertion. He asked how many of those men were tried by commanding officers, and how many by courts martial. I am advised again by the judge advocate general that it would involve a tremendous amount of work to get out the number tried by courts martial. It would be still more diffi-

cult to get information respecting those tried by summary conviction, because that would necessitate going through part II orders for the whole country, from the first occasion upon which such prosecutions were initiated. Figures have been given as to the numbers of men in detention, but the work involved to supply the required answer would be so great that it could not be prepared before the committee rises.
While I am on the matter of sentences, the committee might be interested in having information as to what progress has been made by the board of review, which was discussed yesterday. My information is that up to the present time it has considered 436 cases. It has recommended the immediate remission of the balance of the sentences in 182 cases, remission at a later date in 216 cases, and that no remission be considered at the present time in 38 cases.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) or the hon. member for Lake Centre-perhaps both-asked for a statement as to the legality of confining soldiers in civilian prisons. I have a somewhat lengthy statement in this matter, and I am prepared to give it now. This is the opinion of the judge advocate general:
Under section 69 of the Militia Act, revised statutes of Canada, 1927, chapter 132, the Army Act for the time being in force in Great Britain and not inconsistent with the Militia Act, or the regulations made thereunder, applies to the Canadian army. Power of courts martial to award punishments for offences committed by persons subject to military law, is not restricted by the Militia Act or K.R.' (Can.) and section 44 of the Army Act therefore applies. By this section a general court martial or field general court martial or standing court martial may for certain offences under the Army Act award a sentence of penal servitude for not less than three years, imprisonment with hard labour or without hard labour for a term not exceeding two years, or detention for a term not exceeding two years. A district court martial can award the above, except penal servitude.
By section 58 of the Army Act, where a sentence of penal servitude is passed by a court martial, the military convict shall as soon as practicable be committed to a penal servitude prison to undergo his sentence according to law.
By section 63 (1) of the Army Act, where a sentence of imprisonment is passed by a court martial, the military prisoner shall undergo the term of his imprisonment either in a military prison or in a detention barrack, or in other military custody or in a [Mr. Abbott.l
civil prison, or partly in one way and partly in another.
By order in council P.C. 4769, dated June 23, 1944, . where a sentence of detention is passed by a court martial in Canada upon a soldier or other person subject to military law as a soldier, the military prisoner may undergo the term of such sentence either in a military prison or detention barrack or in other military custody or in a civil prison, or partly in one way and partly in another; provided that no military prisoner so sentenced shall be required to undergo the whole or any part of such sentence in a civil prison unless an adjutant-general or a general or a district officer commanding or the commander of the camp under whose command the military prisoner is for the time being, so orders.
In so far as sentence of penal servitude, imprisonment or detention awarded by a court martial outside Canada are concerned, P.C. 1304 of March 4, 1944, provides that such military prisoner may be transferred or removed to Canada to undergo the sentence or the balance thereof in such place -or places to which he could have been committed to serve such sentence if he had been tried by a court martial and sentenced in any place in Canada. This same order authorizes such prisoner to be kept in military custody or in civil custody or partly in one and partly in the other, as the occasion may require, until he reaches the place in Canada in which he is to undergo his sentence or the balance (hereof.
An order of a competent military authority is under Army Act section 61 (1) sufficient authority for the committal of a military convict, so sentenced to a penal servitude prison.

Mr. Chairman, I hope that the minister and the committee will not feel that I am taking up too much time in making a few observations on matters which are referred to under several headings and therefore cannot be appropriately dealt with under any one of them. Furthermore, the points to which I shall refer were raised directly or indirectly in the minister's remarks of October 16, and were not fully covered then.
First I should like to refer to a series of signal stations which were established up in the Mackenzie River district immediately after the last war, and manned by officers, non-commissioned officers and men of the Royal Canadian Signal Corps. These wireless stations not only provided communication.between the northwest territories and the outside -that is, Canada-but offered a splendid opportunity to the men of the Royal Canadian Signal Corps to gain experience in handling a great deal of traffic.
During the early years of that operation I doubt whether it was at all self-sustaining, but as the settlers, miners and prospectors in

Demobilization-Army
the north became more accustomed to wireless, the revenue from those stations increased. But the point I am most anxious to emphasize is that excellent training was provided for the personnel of the Royal Canadian Signal Corps. To illustrate my point I have only to instance one or two officers who took part in those operations, and call attention to the success that they achieved during the war. I would refer to Captain Young, the first officer to establish a station at Aklavik, who remained in the arctic regions two years, has now risen to the rank of major general, and is the quartermaster general of- the Canadian forces. Other officers who were employed in that service were Major General Weeks, who has recently been recalled from England to do important work with the department here; Brigadier Genet, who was the chief army signal officer during the operations in England and in northwest Europe, and Brigadier Macklin, who is deputy chief of the general staff in England. Other men who were in the ranks in those days have been awarded their commissions during this war as the result of the experience they gained. I do not think anybody can deny that the experience which was gained by those men in the northwest territories was not only valuable to themselves but assisted this country during the war, and that the service provided a very useful means of intercommunication between the northwest territories and the central parts of Canada.
When this war came, further defence projects were undertaken in the northwest. We have the Canol project between Fort Norman and Edmonton, Fort Norman and Whitehorse. Then communication stations were established by the American signal service. Then there was the northwest staging route which ran from Edmonton through Canadian territories, Fort St. John, Whitehorse and on into Alaska. I pay tribute to a small detachment of the Royal Canadian Corps of Signals who carried the load during the early days of the construction of the Alcan highway by sending all messages from Whitehorse to Canada.
As the defences were, increased on the Pacific coast it became necessary to enlarge the communications service in British Columbia, and the Pacific coast system of communications was established. There was a board appointed on which there were representatives of all the three services, and also of the various systems of communications then serving British Columbia, such as the British Columbia Telephones, the Canadian National Railways Telephones, the Canadian Pacific Railway Telephones and the government telephones. It was soon found that the
existing telephone lines were quite inadequate to carry the amount of traffic which was required. New lines had to be built into remote areas. I believe I am correct in saying that the sum of $12,500,000 was devoted to the purpose of improving those communications. Some of that money was spent in reconditioning such systems as the lines of the British Columbia Telephone company between Vancouver and Hope and between Victoria and Campbell River, and also a branch line running to Port Albemi. Other money was spent on improving, or one might almost say reconditioning, the lines of those other companies. In addition to the money which was spent directly by those companies, hundreds of soldiers were employed in clearing the right of way, digging telephone post holes, erecting the poles, and stringing the wires. The amount of money spent on material would have been only a very small fraction of the cost of reconditioning those lines and of building new lines into more remote areas.
I should like to ask the minister one or two questions with regard to this Pacific coast communication * system. Will he give to the men now in the Canadian corps of signals an opportunity to gain the same sort of experience by operating those lines which are now in the more remote areas that the men of the Royal Canadian Corps of Signals gained when they were operating the Yukon northwest territory system? Can the minister tell us, perhaps not to-day, but when the item dealing with signals and wireless is brought down, the amount of money which was paid to the British Columbia Telephones in connection with this Pacific coast communication system, and which was spent in improving or reconditioning those lines belonging to British Columbia Telephones, which I have already mentioned, namely, Vancouver, Hope, Victoria, Campbell River, and the branch line to Alberni?
I should like to ask the minister also what arrangements have been made to dispose of the equipment following the cessation of hostilities. In this case it is not an arrangement which will be made by the War Assets Corporation, since I understand that an arrangement already has been made with the companies as to the manner in which the equipment will be disposed of within some period following the cessation of hostilities. Unless these companies are given some special consideration it is unlikely that they will be able to continue the service in the more remote areas. That service I know has been extended in northern British Columbia to such places as Prince George, Vanderhoof and Prince Rupert; from
Demobilization-Army

Williams Lake to Bella Coola, and in the northern section of Vancouver island running from Campbell River to the very northern point of the island. In addition wireless links have been established between the Queen Charlotte islands and Prince Rupert. If those services could be placed at the disposal of the settlers in the areas concerned I think we might look forward to the same development there that we have seen in the northwest. The fact that there is no communication in a remote area discourages new settlers from going in. These facilities have been provided, and I am very anxious to find out whether they will remain and whether they will be operated by the Royal Canadian corps of signals, thus giving the personnel of that corps the opportunities which proved so valuable when they were operating the chain of communications down the Mackenzie river. Although I cannot speak from any first-hand knowledge I believe there are similar lines in eastern Canada, at least one running along the north shore of the St. Lawrence river. This is an example of what I referred to in my remarks on October 16, when I urged that the post-war army should have an opportunity of being closely linked with industrial life so that the men of the permanent force would 
have a broader outlook on life than the majority of those in the permanent force had before the war started. I believe it is of the utmost importance that the personnel of the permanent force should be closely linked with the industrial and professional life of the country, particularly in view of the fact that in his remarks the Minister of National Defence referred to .the importance he attached to the reserve arm3r, which, though he did not actually say so, I understood would be the backbone of the army of Canada in the future.
Referring to the permanent force of the future, the minister intimated that it would consist of some 20,000 to 25,000 personnel. Would the minister explain what formations or units will make up that force? I do not mind whether he actually names the regiments which will be included, if he will give us an indication of how he arrived at the figure of
20,000	to 25,000, so that the country may have some idea as to the type of standing army it is intended should be maintained in the future. I think it may be extremely unwise at the present time to commit ourselves too definitely for the future, because we are entering into a new era, one which has been sometimes described as the atomic era. As was suggested the other day, it might be more advisable to spend money on scientists rather than on units, and it is important that we should know the pattern of this force which is to consist of some 20,000 to 25,000 men. Will the minister give consideration to the proposal I made that now is the time when we should set up an advisory board to consist of members of all the different services, and representatives of industry, the professions and science, to work out calmly and without haste the type of future army we should have, instead of committing ourselves at this particular time to any definite formations or types of units?

speechtext:
I have taken a note of the questions my hon. friend has asked about the signal system and so on, and will endeavour to answer them when we are discussing item 6, which deals with signals and wireless.
I am asked to give a more definite outline as to how this permanent force will be made up. In my initial statement, as the committee knows, I stated it would number about 20,000 or 25,000. I am glad the hon. member agrees that it is a mistake to be too definite these days as to just how a force will be composed, or what type of formations we shall have. Present plans contemplate the formation of immediately available field forces which, pending a clearer definition of our future military obligations under any world security organization, will consist essentially of a brigade group

Demobilization-Army
augmented by two armoured regiments, one medium artillery battery, together of course with the usual administrative and training elements to assist the reserve army, including a coastal artillery battery on each coast, and a composite anti-aircraft battery. In addition there would be staffs, services and personnel for scientific development.
As some hon. members will probably know, the main element of that proposed brigade group would consist of headquarters, three infantry battalions, a field artillery regiment of three field batteries, an anti-tank battery and a field company of engineers, together with signals, medical and staff units, maintenance workshops and other essential elements.
Broadly speaking, that is the composition of the proposed permanent force element of our post-war army. As I said in my preliminary statement, that army will divide into two parts, a full-time permanently employed active force, and a part-time reserve organization which will reflect the military potential of the country and on present plans, as I said, will consist of a force of six divisions.
As the committee knows, this so-called permanent force will supply full-time personnel for training of the reserve army, including administrative personnel, adjutants, instructors and the like.
I am using the term "permanent force", although I believe I should like to get away from that term. I do not know that the names can as yet be accepted as settled. My preference would be the use of the terms "Canadian army, active force" and "Canadian army, reserve force." However that is a matter which could ut; uicscusstiLi in a. special committee on military affairs, if such committee were set up at the next session. I do not know that the names are particularly important. At the present time what I have set out might be accepted as a satisfactory description of our post-war army. It is one army-a Canadian army with an active force and a reserve force. I have said that I should like to get away from the term "permanent force"; there may be others who would like the use of that term continued.
Mr. PEARIvES: Will what the minister has set out be in addition to the occupational force?

I am sure the members of the committee have been interested in the information just given as to the units and formations of the future permanent force or the future Canadian army. When the minister made his statement, as reported on page 1136 of Hansard, he referred briefly to the proposed future organization of the reserve army. I was very glad indeed to hear the minister say to-day, in reply to a suggestion of the hon. member for Nanaimo, that a review would be made by members of the various branches of the armed services and other persons. That suggestion is set out in more detail by the hon. member, as reported on page 1181 of Hansard.
I hope when the minister does make an announcement as to the future -reserve army he will assure the house of one thing, that our

Demobilization-Army
future reserve army will be maintained and conducted on a most efficient basis. We are all familiar with the methods that were adopted in the past, and we all know of the training, equipment and other matters in connection with reserve army that obtained between 1919 and 1939. I think it is safe to say that during those years all military forces *were starved. During that time in this very chamber various attempts were made by pacifists and others to have our military expenditures reduced to a dollar. Perhaps it was political expediency and the necessity to search for votes, but during those years apparently there were some who had little regard or consideration for the future defence of this country.
How did the Tories vote on that?
The hon. member can make his speech after I have finished.
There were no pacifists among the Conservatives, anyway.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I again remind members of the committee that they must address the Chair.

If the hon. member who has just asked a question would care to look up the records for those years he will have no difficulty in finding to what party the members who made those motions to reduce the estimates belonged.
The officers and men who had the interests of the militia at heart during the years 1919 to 1939 received very little encouragement, either from the public or from National Defence headquarters. I think it is only fair to pay a tribute to those men, because great credit is due them for holding their units together, even on a skeleton basis. The pay was very small, and any officer who maintained his connection with his unit had to pay many of the expenses out of his own pocket. ^The equipment supplied was often quite poor, and there w'as little assistance from the public. It was often quite difficult to get recruits. For example, the tendency in those years was to have the grants for cadet training reduced. All this hindered and hampered the non-permanent active militia. In many cases the unit was scattered over one or two counties, and no consideration was given to the payment of travelling expenses incurred by the men and officers who had to travel some distance to take their training. In short, it appeared during those years that every possible hindrance and obstruction was
being placed in the way of Canada's having an active and efficient non-permanent active force.
In 1939 war broke out. The number of men in the permanent force was quite small, and practically all of them were engaged in administrative or instructional duties. All that Canada had was a non-permanent active militia, and yet in record time the units that were ordered to mobilize were able to recruit up to strength. The officers used their skeleton staffs and were able to achieve this result. Officers, N.C.O.'s and men who had obtained some training or had attended courses under the non-permanent set-up proved to be the backbone of our army m the early days of 1939.
We all recall the great lack of qualified instructors in the early days of the war, and I think that due credit has never been given to those officers, N.C.O.'s and men of the nonpermanent active militia who did so much in the early days of the war to start building up our magnificent Canadian army. The nonpermanent active militia units which were instructed to mobilize and form various Canadian divisions were able through their second battalions to keep a steady stream of partly-trained reinforcements enlisting for the active arm}'.
I realize, Mr. Chairman, that most of this is past history, but it is important to learn at least one small lesson from our neglect of the reserve army between the two wars, and to point out how easy it will be in the years that lie ahead again to slip back into the same inefficient conditions that existed after the last war. For Canada to maintain a permanent force and a reserve army along the lines outlined by the minister will cost considerable money, and I venture to say that in time there will be attempts made to pare and chisel down the estimates for both the permanent and the reserve army.
When the minister considers the set-up for the reserve army I hope he will keep in mind one matter which is of great importance to the soldier, and that is the question of pay. In the reserve army, in between the two wars, when a man went to camp with his unit he received very small pay. In many cases he was making a financial sacrifice which he could ill afford. I suggest to the minister that there be some extension of the time spent in camp each year. Under the old system of two weeks' training in camp, one day was spent going to camp, another day returning home, one day in getting settled, a day of sports, a day for general inspection, and at least one or two days when wet weather
Demobilization-Army

interfered with training plans. Thus few days were left for training. As the minister well knows, outside of the larger centres, the men in these rural units have their platoons and companies scattered throughout the smaller towns and villages.
As to equipment, I was very glad to hear the minister say that there would be no shortage of the finest and best equipment for the reserve army in the future. I am sure that the minister realizes that one of the best and easiest ways of interesting young men in the reserve army of the future is by assuring them of proper training with the finest and most up to date equipment that is available.
I suggest further to the minister that much could be done in the various armouries in the way of sports and recreation and club activities during the winter months, all of which have a tendency to hold the unit together and prove of interest to the men. If the reserve army is made attractive, the minister will have no difficulty in attracting to the various units many officers, N.C.O.'s and men who have served in this war, officers and men who will be a credit to the unit and who by their interest and their experience will be the means of bringing our reserve army up to a very high standard of efficiency.
I suggest to the minister that he give most serious consideration to the matter of promotions for both officers and men in the reserve army. In the past, promotion has often been very slow, and as a result the unit often lost many capable men. I do not know what the present educational standard of the department is before a man can be recommended for a commission. I know that it used to be that the candidate had to have at least junior matriculation. If that is still the standard, I hope the minister will consider whether, there should not be some lowering of that standard. I should like to cite to him the case of two N.C.O.'s who belonged to the Hastings and Prince Edward regiment prior to 1939. Both enlisted in September, 1939, and proceeded overseas in December, 1939. At the date of their enlistment neither of these two men had attended school beyond the fourth book; yet both were recommended for commissions after they had been overseas for some time, and both qualified and both went through long periods of heavy fighting. Both gained for themselves a very enviable record. One has recently returned home with the rank of major and a decoration, and the other is now a captain serving in the army of occupation. It seems to me that men who show the ability to handle men and have initiative and a keen interest in military affairs should not be penal-fMr. G. S. White.]
ized and deprived of promotion and the advantage of taking an officers' course simply because during their school days they were not fortunate enough to have obtained a certain educational certificate.
In making his statement the minister said at page 1136 of Hansard:
It is intended to assist commanding officers of reserve army units in the training and administration of their personnel by providing for each unit full time (active force) officers and other ranks on an adequate scale.
I take it from this that each reserve unit will have a permanent full-time administrative and training staff. If that is the correct interpretation, I wish to congratulate the minister, because, as he probably realizes, the administrative side of the unit is most important, and in many cases it has been found almost too much for an officer on part time to handle.
I think the minister will agree that there are many features about the reserve army as it has been constituted in the past and is now constituted that could be improved upon. I hope that he will not altogether follow the present pattern of organization of the reserve army, for, after all, the methods and the organization that we had in 1939 are hardly suitable for 1945 and the future, because science and mechanization have changed the whole picture.
I suggest to the minister that our whole future defence policy be very carefully planned before he adopts any plan for our future reserve army. I hope the minister will not miss this opportunity to reorganize our reserve army on a basis that will provide properly for our future defence and that in the reorganization he will make the reserve army attractive to thousands of men who have served in the armed forces during this war.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I thank my hon. friend for his very valuable contribution. He has made a number of most useful suggestions, and I can assure him that they .will receive careful consideration. The question of the reserve army and the changes which will be made is still one that is very much open. As I indicated in my statement, it is proposed to consult the various defence associations with respect to it. I agree that there is plenty of room for improvement in the reserve army, as in most other things, and we welcome suggestions from any source, particularly from one who, like my hon. friend the member for Hastings-Peterborough, had extensive experience in the reserve army before the war.

Mr. Chairman, one of the very first things that we have to decide in this house on all sides is whether or not we

Demobilization-Army
are prepared to back plans for the defence of Canada. It becomes almost unbearable to sit and listen to a number of Progressive Conservative members such as one of .their financial experts who in a speech on the floor of the house this year indicated the most dismal outlook with respect to financing the future defence of Canada. There is not the slightest idea or concept of any new way of financing the expenditures necessary to maintain an adequate armed force in Canada. I believe it would be a very fine thing if our Progressive Conservative friends would, devote their attention to this matter of where the money would come from. If once they will settle that, I do not think there will be any doubt at all about the minister bringing in a programme to build up as fine a defence force as we all desire. Canada has proved herself beyond peradven-ture able to produce all the goods and services and all the men and women necessary to provide the kind of fighting force which this country needs to discharge her responsibility in the dangerous times which lie ahead in the next few years. But Canada's leadership has not shown that it knows how to find the money with which to use those resources and those men and women. There is where the difficulty lies.
I .wish to ask the minister one or two questions about another matter. If we are to have a permanent force-as we are-it becomes necessary that we make conditions just as good for that force as possible. It was conveyed to me in a letter the other day that in the permanent force which was in Canada before the war the number of men permitted to marry was limited. I wonder if that is true. I am told that no more than about fifteen per cent of the permanent men were permitted to marry. Is that true?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I believe that is correct. I believe there was a married establishment; I do not know just what it was.

Then I think the minister will be the first to recognize that the condition which obtained was unsound. If there is anything we want in Canada, and want desperately, it is babies, and we want them right away. At the present rate of falling off of the birth rate in the Anglo-Saxon world it is going to be under an exceedingly difficult handicap in twenty-five years to meet its potential foes. We may just as well face that fact; and I submit, Mr. Chairman, that if hon. members are not prepared to face that fact and take whatever measures are necessary to meet the situation, they will be in large measure betraying their trust. Certainly if, when we take a considerable number of our young men and put them
in our permanent force, we impose such conditions that they are unable to marry, we shall be defeating one of the objectives we ought to have. May I suggest to the minister that measures be taken to permit those who desire to marry so to do, notwithstanding that they are in the permanent force, and furthermore, that adequate measures be taken to enable them to support a family while they are in the permanent force.

It would be composed of men who, because of their occupation or the distances they live from urban centres, would probably not be able to take advantage of training in the reserve army. It is generally felt that the training they would receive in the proper use of fire arms, in the building up of self-reliance and so on would be of great value to the country as a whole. I would ask the minister to make a statement now with regard to the matter. If he cannot do that, I ask him to give consideration to it.
Before I sit down I should like to ask another question in connection with the P.C.M.R. This has to do with the request that has been made that they be permitted to retain the rifles which were issued to them when the organization was formed. In reply to a question asked on September 12 by the hon. member for Nanaimo the minister made the statement that the members of the P.C.M.R. would be allowed to retain the 30-30 carbine that had been issued. He stated that this matter had been taken up with the Department of Munitions and Supply and that instructions would be issued by the War Assets Corporation allowing these men to retain these rifles perhaps on the payment of a nominal sum. That statement created general satisfaction on the part of those who had 30-30 rifles.
However, it created some dissatisfaction on the part of those who had been issued with the other form of rifle, the 30-06. I and other members from British Columbia have had requests from these men or on behalf of these men that they be allowed to keep their 30-06 rifles on the payment of a nominal sum. Objection may be raised that the 30-06 is not a purely sporting rifle, such as the 30-30, but I would point out that it is not a regular Canadian army issue. It was an obselete United States army rifle which was brought into Canada at the time this organization was formed. The new pattern of the Enfield rifle has since been produced in a standardized form for the Canadian army, and I think there is some justification for the case put forward by these men. They would not be keeping army equipment if they were allowed to retain their 30-06 rifle.
One other objection that might be raised is that considerable feeling has been created against the indiscriminate possession of firearms. I should like to point out that the Pacific coast militia rangers, who were all volunteers, have been in possession of their rifles for some years, and they have not been

Demobilization-Army
guilty of any of the offences which have caused this feeling to spring up in recent months. If they were to be trusted with their rifles in times of war, when they were giving their services without any remuneration, it is difficult to understand why they should have them taken away now.
In view of the excellent volunteer service without pay that these men rendered, in view of the widespread requests which have been made, I would appreciate it very much if the minister could make a statement in reply to these two questions. First, can they be continued in some voluntary form? Second, will he give further consideration to allowing them to retain their rifles on the payment of a nominal sum?

I do not want to repeat what the hon. member for Kamloops has said, but I suggest that the minister reconsider this matter. As I understand it, the rifle known as the 30-06 is being sold in every hardware store in the state of Washington. The answer given before by the minister was that this was a military rifle and could not be sold, but I think-that answer is inconsistent when they are available so easily in hardware stores.
Before the minister took charge of this department-I am sorry he did not- take charge before-the people on the Pacific coast and in eastern Canada were afraid at one time that the Japs might invade the Pacific coast. We depended upon these people who served in this organization. There were farmers' sons, farmers themselves, and people in every class of life on the coast who served in this organization. They had no hope of reward; they
were given no uniforms; they had no rifles and they provided their own* equipment. No such action was ever taken in the interior of Canada, and particularly in* eastern Canada.
These men made that effort, and I think a grateful government and a grateful people should at least allow them to retain these rifles. I understand this is the United States rifle with the red band and it is regarded as being useless for anything. These rifles should be made available to these people through War Assets Corporation. When I read in the coast newspaper that what is known* as the Fairmile, a small boat costing $195,000, can be sold for $3,000 to a few sporting gentlemen who came here from England, do not tell me that we cannot afford to sell these rifles for $5.
There is one other matter that I wish to mention. I do not class myself as a spokesman for the army, but I am very proud to have been an army representative, and I want to tell the army through you, Mr. Chairman, and this committee, that they are very fortunate in not having as minister of national defence a major-general or a brass hat of any kind. Instead they have a gunner; in other words, what is commonly called a private, as Minister of National Defence.
I wish to ask the minister a question because of some information I received which I assume is correct because it was contained in a return that was brought down in the house, sessional paper No. 172, with respect to leave in the armed sendees. My first question had to do with air force leave. I want to make myself ptaueciiy dear; i do not want to detract in any way from the service that the air force has given to this country, nor do I want to curtail in any shape or form any leave or pass or allowance that may now be allowed to them. But I do want to insist that anything that is given to the air force must also be given to the men of the army, the men who actually won this war. You can talk about your atomic bomb, but all the atomic bombs in the world will not win a war without the infantry. This was my question, appearing in sessional paper No. 172, and I want this on Hansard because the idea apparently of bringing down the information in a return is so that nobody will know anything about it. 2.	Do (a) naval and (b) army personnel receive the same leave for equivalent service?

I want to make it perfectly clear that I have every respect for the air force and for the navy; but I have no respect-I shall have to modify that and say that I have no confidence in any department that will do something for the air force which they will not do for the fighting men of the army. I want to tell you, Mr. Chairman, and, through you, the members of the legion across Canada, that the reason the air force got away with so much in the past was that the member for Quebec South fought for his department when he was minister for air, and I insist that the minister must see to it that if the air force gets twenty-eight days leave the army must have it too, in the future.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I shall have to look into this leave question. I will agree that there should not be any distinction between the three services. It may be more apparent than real, as the answer in the return says. The distinction only lies between the army in Canada and the other services, not as regards the men who served overseas. The men who serve at N.D.H.Q., for instance, have a pretty good chance to get forty-eight hour leaves, and the same applies to men serving all over Canada. There is a proper distinction in the matter of leave to be made between those serving in Canada and the men returning from overseas. I will look into the question so far as the navy is concerned. I can only say at the moment that the leave procedure in the navy is a bit different. Most of the navy personnel are on one coast or the other serving in ships, and they cannot get forty-eight hours leave or whatever other leaves the men in the army can get. For that reason it may be they get a bit longer leave on discharge or its equivalent in pay. But I will look into the whole leave situation and see if I can give a more specific answer before these estimates are passed. .

The N.R.M.A. man the minister is talking about is the man who decided to stay in Canada. This man did not do that; he was requisitioned for this service and put there. He was given no option as to whether he would go in the army or go overseas or go anywhere else. To begin with, his age was against him; he should not have been called up. He was more essential in the employment in which he was engaged, for a great many men are not physically capable of that kind of employment. The minister must remember that, later, coal miners were frozen to their jobs, they were not allowed to enlist; and this man was called from an . essential job, where he was earning fairly good money, and dealt with under government regulations. Regardless of how you quibble about departments or where the responsibility lies, in the final analysis it was under government regulations that he was called up; he served two years and did what he was told; he did not refuse to go anywhere; and I think the least that can be done for that man when he goes out is to give him a clothing allowance to enable him to get a new outfit for himself. The rehabilitation regulations as applied to a man who served in Canada but would have gone overseas had they wanted him to go over should be applicable to that particular classification. I think a great injustice has been done to people in this category. The Minister of National Defence, as an old soldier and as one who, as the hon. member for Eraser Valley has pointed out, served in a low classification, should certainly appreciate the position in which that man finds himself in going back to his family and trying to .reestablish himself. Something should be done for him. I trust the Minister of National Defence will join with the Minister of Justice in urging the treasury board to relax the purse-strings and do something for the very small group who are in this position. The cost would not amount to very much.

speechtext: That Vias not yet been decided; it is under consideration at the moment. I am pleased to hear that it is under consideration. I hope that the minister will give it favourable consideration.
My other question has to do with the veterans' guard. Certain companies of the veterans' guard have been disbanded, while other personnel of that guard have been demobilized; but there are still a fairly large number, I think two or three thousand, veterans of the great war of 1914-18 who are still serving the country in the veterans' guard.
As is generally known, the veterans' guard was called into existence partly to act as guards over German prisoners of war in this country, and partly to guard vulnerable points. I should like to point out to the committee that the duty was well done and that those old soldiers of the first great war carried on under sometimes quite trying and difficult circumstances in guarding the various vulnerable points, magazine areas and prisoners of war camps. There is some concern amongst some of the personnel of the veterans' guard who still remain as to whether they are suddenly to be turned out on to the street. They would like to have an opportunity of finishing the job they started, namely, the guarding of prisoners of war. Their concern results from the fact that some of the companies have already .been disbanded. They have the fear that they might be turned out on to the street just as winter is beginning. Very few of those old veterans have any great value in the labour market. Will the guard be retained as part of the interim army? Is consideration being given to its further perpetuation as, perhaps one might describe it, the guard of army commissionaires. There are a great many tasks to be performed in a peace-time army, such as

Demobilization-Army
guards on camps, on rifle ranges, caretakers at armouries, and so forth. Would the minister give consideration to perpetuating the name of this corps composed of soldiers of the two wars, the majority of whom are now getting well up in years, and have them perform the tasks to which I refer?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Of course I cannot make any definite statement as to just how many we - shall retain from the companies of the veterans' guard. As my hon. friend has said, they performed exceedingly valuable services during this war and they are still continuing to perform them. There are still some of them here at National Defence headquarters; others are guarding German prisoners of war, and others are guarding other types of government property. They are performing very useful work. There is no immediate prospect of there being a substantial reduction, at any rate, in the number of the veterans' guard during the next few months, certainly not during the winter months to which my hon. friend has referred. As a matter of fact we are actually taking into the guard some veterans of this war, not a great many, and it is expected that we shall continue to use ' them for some little time to come. I do not know that I would say that they would form part of the so-called interim force. I use that term more in describing the type of man who enlists for our permanent post-war army, and there are considerations of age and all that sort of thing, with the pension entitlement that goes with it, that have to be taken into account. But we shall certainly continue to utilize the services of the veterans' guard sc long as they can be usefully employed.

There is another question which bothers me. We are passing estimates for the Department of National Defence (Army). I believe every hon. member is aware that since the war the system has developed whereby officers, noncommissioned officers and men have been seconded to other departments for duty. My personal opinion is that there should be no seconding of officers and men to other branches of the government; that once those officers are seconded to another branch of the government they should be struck off the army strength. To-night we are voting money for pay and allowances for the army, some of which money is to go to officers and men 47696-110
serving other departments of the government. I would ask the minister how many officers and other ranks are seconded from his department to other government departments. I would ask also why these officers should not be struck off the strength of the army and transferred to the departments to which they have been seconded. I would offer the suggestion that the reason they are not struck off the strength of the army is that through their army pay and allowances they are getting a great deal more than they would receive in the branch to which they have been seconded.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
To answer the latter part of the question first, according to the latest reports there is a total of 161 seconded in Canada, as follows: to the Department of Munitions and Supply, sixteen; to the joint inspection board of the United Kingdom and Canada, forty; to other boards, eighteen; to various other government departments, forty-two. Then there are medical officers seconded for civilian purposes. My hon. friend may recall that we sometimes lend some medical officers either to other government departments, such as the Department of Veterans Affairs, or temporarily to districts which are badly in need of medical assistance. There are thirty-two medical officers seconded in this way; and miscellaneous, thirteen. We are trying to get that number down as quickly as possible. A good many of the departments to which these officers are seconded require them in a military capacity, and the work they are performing is primarily military. Another reason which is oerhaps more a practical reason than anything else, is that these officers would not be prepared to serve in these other departments except as officers. If they are to be employed as civilians they will go back to their own civilian jobs. I can assure the committee that every effort is being made to reduce as much as possible the number of officers seconded to other departments. Under present regulations they are required to wear civilian clothes when serving in such departments.

Perhaps that would give my hon. friend a fair indication of what is considered to be the probable number. I can get the actual number, but he will appreciate that it

varies from day to day. I .will get the latest figure and put it on the record.

I also wanted to say a word about, the veterans' guard, to which I was very glad to hear the minister pay, tribute. These men have done a magnificent job for this country. Most of them are elderly men who will find it very difficult to reestablish themselves in industry. We have in Canada many camps which will be closed or partly closed down but which will have to be looked after, and I would suggest to the minister that in a camp like Camp Borden, for instance, which can never be used one hundred per cent in peace time except for summer training, two or three companies of the veterans' guard could be employed in maintenance. These men served us well in war time. Many of them presumably will be discharged in a few months. I believe we should try to do something to retain their services, and I suggest to the minister that wherever he may need caretakers, if you care to call them that, or engineer companies or employment companies in the maintenance of these camps, which will be used in future as militia camps, he employ the services of the veterans' guard. I believe this is a sound suggestion and it would be fair to, these men, because in my opinion they cannot get reestablished in the labour market. Unless the government is prepared to pay these men a pension on which they can live for the rest of their lives, they will have to be looked after in some other way, and this might be a good way for the government to do it.

I think the committee
should make a better recommendation for the veterans guard than mereljr trying to find jobs, especially in an economy where jobs are going to be pretty hard to find, even for the young veterans who are coming back.
,1 became acquainted with many of the men who were in the veterans guard in the last four years. I knew some of these men before war broke out in 1939, and I found that, so far as their economic life was Qoncerned, the war to them was in a certain sense a blessing, because it gave them an income. They came back from one war, after helping to make the world a place fit for heroes to live in, and at that time they found it very difficult to rehabilitate themselves. Then, when this war came along they were not of an age which would permit their giving service in the active-army, with the result that, as we all agree, they performed a great service to Canada in other ways. We should not ask them to rehabilitate themselves once again, at a time when it will be even harder, I am convinced, than it was following the last war. If we rehabilitate the young men who were in this war, and the young men who were in the war industries-and the young women-I am quite satisfied the country can produce enough wealth to retire all the veterans of the last war on a satisfactory living income. The committee should consider nothing less than that. Anything less would do honour neither to ourselves nor to the veterans guard.
Mr. COCKERAIvI: I have one further question in connection with pay and allowances. Why does the department consider it necessary to give those officers extended leave, and why - do they not employ them to the extent to which they should be employed? speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
That policy is in fact being carried out as quickly as possible. My hon. friend will realize, however, that we are still in a stage of transition, and that demobilization is quite active. I should like to bring to the attention of the minister and also to that of the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) two matters which have been brought to my attention from a soldier overseas whose name, in accordance with custom, I shall not divulge. The first deals with khaki college. Thus far I do not think any statement has been made by the minister respecting the set-up of khaki college, and the situation in connection with teachers in that organization. My information is that there is a shortage of teachers in that college. My informant holds the view that army men will not volunteer their services to teach. He asks why a private, corporal or other N.C.O. who is at present awaiting repatriation, and doing relatively nothing, should teach at the college
Demobilization-Army

for his usual rate of pay, plus a lot of hard work and plus postponement of his repatriation. Perhaps the minister would make a statement on this matter.
The other suggestion made by my correspondent has to do with the matter of recognizing those men and women in various parts of Europe who risked their lives and liberty to aid Canadian nationals to escape from the Germans during the period of war. As the minister knows, there are thousands of our airmen who were sfiot down but who subsequently were passed back to England, through underground channels. The United Kingdom does give some recognition to those, men and women of the underground, and I would ask the minister to consider whether or not this country might follow suit. Most hon. members have had friends who have received the benefit of this special help in their escape from enemy territory. I would ask the minister at the appropriate time to indicate the government's policy in that regard.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
There is no shortage of teaching staff for this session of the khaki college, but it is anticipated we may have some difficulty in the next one. The point my hon. friend makes is a good one, and it is receiving constant attention.

We have not yet in Canada any special order of chivalry which would seem appropriate. I would assume the services to which he has referred are not the kind which might properly be recognized in a monetary way.

Several days ago I directed a question to the Minister of National Defence with respect to the treatment being given to men and women of the three services who had returned from overseas but who had not received disembarkation leave because they had been called, either by the Department of Veterans Affairs or by some industry holding priority rights, to take civil employment. At that time the minister informed me that effective April 19 of this year all persons who had been discharged on this basis would receive thirty days pay in lieu of leave. The minister also said at that time that the reason why April 19 was set as the cut-off day was that prior to that time no requests had been received in connection with this matter of pay in lieu of leave. In the event of its being found that requests had been received prior

to April 19, will the minister take action in this connection, the various orders in council and regulations notwithstanding? *

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I do not remember using the phrase that no requests had been received. W'hat I had in mind was that there had been no substantial number of these cases. When the clothing allowances were increased they became effective after the date the new regulation came into effect. To my knowledge there was certain correspondence before April 19 on behalf of men in the service Who had come back to take posts with the Department of Veterans Affairs. It seems to me the minister was remiss in not considering those cases before he set the cut-off date of April 19. speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It was not because of any particular case; I simply used that case as an illustration of the desirability of putting it into effect.
I misunderstood the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services

For the information of the minister I may say that the Department of Veterans Affairs brought back a block of overseas veterans, and as far as I am aware none of them received thirty days pay in lieu of discharge leave.

We hope.

Before we leave pay and allowances I will ask the minister one more question. I do not like to pester him and drag him back over the trail, but a great deal of this discussion has ranged' around the position of men discharged, perhaps for misconduct, and serving one, two or three years. The dependents of that particular classification of soldier lose their pay and allowances. A man who is discharged from the service, particularly back in Canada, and incarcerated in a civilian penitentiary, and who, as many of them are, is married and has a family, is in a bad position, much worse than that of the ordinary civilian prisoner. If he were a civilian prisoner the municipal authorities would accept responsibility, but in a matter of this kind the municipal authorities, at least in the sections *with which I am acquainted, take the stand that this is a military matter; the Canadian government requisitioned the man for service; he got in difficulties; he was sentenced by a military court martial; he is in gaol as a military prisoner, and the government should accept some responsibility. I think the municipal authorities are justified in taking that stand.
Demobilization-Army

iYhat I have in mind is this. There is a branch of the pay and allowances organization known as the supplementary grants branch. Where there are extenuating circumstances and the soldier's pay does not cover any abnormal expenditure his dependents may run into, the allowance can be supplemented. The machinery is there; the supplementary grants branch is set up, and there is a board of administration. I am, wondering if there is not a possibility of having a wife and children in this categoiy brought within the sphere of these supplementary grants and given some allowance until such time as the courts martial have reviewed the case and a final disposition is made of it. Certainly we have.some responsibility to that family. The reason I am raising the matter now is that it has been up for a week or so and the minister should have had some opportunity of consulting his departmental officials. The matter is one of immediacy, because there are women and children who have been waiting months. Some of them are writing to me, and it is a tough business to have to reply saying that nothing is being done about the matter. This is some-. thing which we could remedy, and very quickly. It is merely a matter of the department making the decision. No new machinery will have to be set up; there is an appropriation of money for allowances, and the purposes for which the grants were originally intended are becoming fewer, as men are discharged from the service. Could the minister give us an assurance that some immediate relief will be given to families in this categoiy?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
The present provisions are that so long as a man is in the service, even if he is detained, the dependents' allowances are continued by the dependents' allowances board for six months. Thereafter the dependents' board of trustees has authority to continue allowances in needy cases. If a man is discharged from the service for misconduct he and his family are in the same position as any other civilians, and if the family are in need they must be taken care of by the local municipal or provincial authorities. Frankly, though, I suppose the matter is arguable. I find it hard to see why a fund which is set up to care for the dependents of well-behaved soldiers should be availed of indefinitely to care for the dependents of others. That charge should properly be placed on the shoulders of perhaps another group of taxpayers. In the final analysis it has to be borne; and of course should be borne by some body of taxpayers. Whether'it should be the federal taxpayer, or whether it should be the local municipal or provincial taxpayer is, of course, a question.
(Mr. Gillis.J
I will give the matter consideration, but up to the present I have always felt that that was a perfectly fair and equitable way of treating these cases. However, I am willing to reconsider it.

I am depending to a large extent on the minister to do something about this matter, but the answer he just gave me does not leave me very much hope. He has. said as head of the department that he thinks the matter as handled at present is fair and equitable. That is not so. Remember that in the first place you requisitioned this man for service. I know of a young man wTho served five years in the Royal Canadian Air Force. He was discharged from that force last April. Under the call-up system he was immediately called into the army. speechtext: I might say to the hon. member for Prince Edward-Lennox that he was not entirely out of order. He wanted certain information as to which- department was responsible for payment. I think he received the information which he sought.
He did not, because I believe the minister will say that it is not his responsibility.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Perhaps we can clear up this confused question. We do the work in the army, that is the clerical work to determine how much gratuity he is entitled to; but the method of payment of the-gratuity is determined as a matter of policy by the Minister of Veterans Affairs, and when I say it is determined by him it is determined by the government as a whole. But it is the responsibility of the Minister of Veterans Affairs and his advisers to decide as to the manner in which gratuities should be paid. Since, however, the army has the records, in the case of a soldier, and the air force has the records in the case of an airman, they make the computation and tell the Department of Veterans Affairs how much the gratuity is. From then on it is the job of the Department of Veterans Affairs, and it is charged not to the vote of the army or of the air force but to the vote of the Department of Veterans Affairs. Have I made that clear?

Take the case of a man who has been in the air force and who afterwards joined the army. I had such a case brought to my attention the other day. When the man was discharged from the army he was not given the credit to which he was entitled from the air force. In applying for his gratuity he was given credit only for the five months he had been in the army. There does not seem to be the coordination there should be.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
That is possible; I will accept that. It may well be that there is a certain lack of coordination, and I will see that it is looked into. Obviously the man is entitled to his gratuity for service both in the air force and in the army. It may be that the staff work is poor in the army or in the air force, but if at the outset he does not. get all he is entitled to he will get it on appeal. I may say we are having some difficulty getting trained staff to get out these cheques as quickly as we would like. My parliamentary assistant tells me that he has not received his gratuity cheque yet, and he has been out of the army for some time. However, we are

Demobilization-Army
doing the best we can and gradually we are catching up. The main difficulty is the question of records and getting sufficient good staff to get out the cheques promptly.

A few minutes ago the minister, in replying to a question I asked, made a statement to which I took exception, when he said I asked the question in my usual courteous manner. I do not know whether or not he was being sarcastic, but certainly I have tried to ask questions in the way they should be asked.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I assure my hon. friend that his questions are always couched in the most courteous and friendly tone. We have known each other for a long time and I would not for a moment suggest anything else.

There was one thing in which I thought the minister was a little precipitous just now; that was when the hon. member for Kingston City brought up the question of the housing of permanent force people. That is a question which is concerned with pay and allowances, because housing is definitely part of the pay and allowances of men who serve in the army.
No.
Lodging, fuel and light are part of the perquisites of the army.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: We pay him, but he has to find them.

That may be so;
but actually if you -have a government-owned house which is rented by an officer, non-commissioned officer or man in the army, you charge him in accordance with the pay he receives for his rank, which is the right way to do it. But the onus is upon the department to see that the members of the permanent force are quartered and housed.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: In peace time; but in war time we cannot make any distinction.

We are in peace time.
' Mr. ABBOTT: In theory, yes; but in effect we are still under war conditions.

I should like to ask one further question, because I am afraid I did not make my point quite clear. That is my fault rather than that of the minister. I asked for consideration, and that is not the word I should have used. During the war, whether we liked it or not, the impression got around that the air force and certain other services received preferential treatment as compared with the army. The direct question I am asking is not whether consideration will be given, but whether the army will be
given exactly the same treatment as to leave, pay and any other allowances that is given any other branch of the service.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Leave conditions vary in all the services, and I cannot say that the army will be given exactly the same treatment. But I do say that they should receive substantially comparable treatment, and that is what they are receiving now, or so I am advised.

If I may ask the minister another question, does he consider seven days leave given since September 17, not before, comparable treatment with thirty days leave given in the air force? I am asking the minister again, will he give the army the same treatment that is given any other branch of the service in connection with leave or otherwise?	.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
The leave we are discussing is a complicated question. We are fighting the battle of the boys who fought in Canada, as far as the army is concerned. None of these personnel to whom my hon. friend is referring served overseas. They are the men to whom he has referred on previous occasions as men who perhaps should not be treated on the same basis as the men who have served abroad, and I think we agree on that. These men have had other opportunities for leave. I understand-and I have seen it myself- that leave regulations have been fairly generous in Canada as far as personnel at National Defence headquarters or district headquarters or anywhere else are concerned. I do not know whether the air force has been a little more generous. In a sense the operations of the air force in Canada are more of an operational character than is the case in connection with the army, because they are flying personnel, and so on. In any event the regulations, as they now stand, provide that men from overseas get this thirty days disembarkation leave when they return. In the navy special leave regulations apply. They get an annual leave; they get certain weekend leaves and twenty-eight days once a year, which they have to take. In the army there is a regular series of leaves: annual leave, week-end leave, and so on, but there is no additional leave on discharge for men who have served in Canada only. Under a recent provision seven days leave may be given. That is not a leave as of right; it is given in order to facilitate discharge procedure, where men are coming back to the depot in large numbers; their documents may not be ready or something like that, and they can be put out on seven days leave. That is the way it- stands, and I do not believe it will be changed.
Demobilization-Army

I should like to follow that a little farther. According to the information contained in that return the minister has been misinformed. Am I to understand from the minister that a member of the groundcrew of the air force who served in England, Belgium or anywhere else, or a man from air force headquarters is to be given preferential treatment to a man in the army who served at Arnhem or somewhere else? Will the man in the army who carried on in the front line be given exactly the same treatment as any other branch of the service?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Oh, yes. He is given exactly the same treatment; there is no difference whatever.

Before the Minister of Veterans Affairs interrupted a few moments ago I had direoted a straight question to the Minister of National Defence, which he did not answer. Would he answer that question now?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I am sorry; would the hon. member mind repeating the question?
Is the minister's department taking any steps to provide adequate living quarters for the wives and families of members of the permanent force; and, if so, what is being done?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I answered that question by saying that it has nothing whatever to do with the item under consideration.
It is pay and allowances.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: No, it has nothing to do with it. We do not provide living quarters for any service personnel. The question of providing housing comes under another department of government; it is primarily a civil responsibility. The hon. member for Kingston City said that the member of the permanent force to whom he had referred had nine children. Well, he seems to be following the precepts of the hon. member for Lethbridge; but he gets the family allowance; he gets the dependents' allowance; he gets subsistence if he is not living' in barracks; he gets his pay and all the rest of it at active force rates, and out of that he is supposed to provide his living accommodation. If there is not living accommodation available he takes his chance the same as every other soldier in Canada, permanent force or whatever he may be.
Presumably the permanent force will get back to permanent force rates of pay. '

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Probably they will.

If they do, they have
a lodgings, fuel and light allowance. I suggest that this is a case which should come under-

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I am going to answer that. The whole question of pay and allowances for the permanent force is now under consideration. There were rates in force before the war. The same rates will not continue after the war. Whether there will be a lodgings, fuel and light allowance is, I think, extremely doubtful.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
On October 1, through
the medium of the order paper I asked certain questions relating to certain enlisted men from M.D. No. 10 who were detailed to do work for the Canadian National Railways near Armstrong, Ontario. My questions at that time had to do with the pay these men were given. I have two reasons for the inquiry I am now making. First I would like to know whether the policy of detailing enlisted men to do this kind of work had definitely been changed, and my second question arises out of the understanding the men had that they would benefit by the higher wages paid by the railway for the work they were doing. On October 1 I asked the minister what these men were paid for their work, and his reply was that during the period they did this work for the Canadian National Railways they received full pay and allowances, including dependents' allowances. I also asked what the railway company paid for the work, and I was told that they paid fifty-three cents for each working hour per soldier, less $5.75 a week per soldier charged for board and lodging. Then I asked to whom the railway company paid the money, and the answer was that it was paid to the receiver general of Canada.
I would remind the minister that I have asked two questions. The first is this: Has the detailing of enlisted men for this kind of work been abolished?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
My second question is:
Do the men themselves benefit in any way from the larger amount of money paid for their work by the railway than the amount they received in pay and allowances?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Well, the policy was
changed. We do not detail men any more. If in essential industries, they are put on extended leave and, under those circumstances, they are paid the regular pay for the work they are doing.
As to whether the men receive any benefit or not, under the conditions outlined by the hon. member the man would get his army

D e mobiliza lion-A rmy
pay, plus full allowances, whether he worked or not. If weather conditions are such that under normal conditions he would not be paid, nevertheless if as h soldier he is detailed, he would continue to receive his daily rate of pay and his allowance. But that policy has now been discontinued, and for work such as that in logging camps, packing plants or construction industries we will put men on extended leave, and they are then hired by the employers at regular rates.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
In this instance no part
of the money paid, to the receiver general of Canada was, in turn, given to the mem or to a regimental or canteen fund?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: No.

In reply to a question
asked by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) on October 25, it was stated that 276 men of the forestry corps were working on the limits or constructing camps for A. D. McGibbon and Sons and C. G. Turner, Esquire. What is the justification at this time for having men wearing uniforms working in civilian camps, especially in view of the fact that the soldiers are working for the defeated member who ran in that riding. This is a serious matter, and the minister should give some consideration to it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: There is a question on the order paper on this point. The answer is about ready, and the information is being prepared. It will probably be put on Hansard to-morrow or, if I have the information to-morrow, I will give it to the committee.
Is it the intention to keep men in uniform working for-

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: No, no. I think, generally speaking, it is just in operations which are being wound up. I announced the policy only a moment ago.

I should like to ask a question on the subject of allowances to servicemen's wives who are still overseas. The minister has told us to-night that about a month ago the government passed an order in council which will take care of the allowances for a discharged man's wife who is still overseas. Is that order in council retroactive, and will wives of servicemen who were discharged b'efore it was passed also receive their allowances until they reach their destination in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It is not retroactive, but applies from the date it was passed which, I believe, was some time in September.

Is the government considering taking care of the wives of the many servicemen who have already been discharged from the service, and whose wives in England, France, Holland or Belgium were receiving no allowance prior to the passage of that order in council?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: They are all receiving it now, automatically; they do not have to make ajjplication for it. There may be the odd case where they have not been traced, but there is no doubt as to their entitlement. If there is any wife still in Europe whose husband has returned to Canada and has been discharged from the army, and who is just kept there because of a lack of shipping, she is entitled to receive dependents' allowances for herself and her children. That is automatic. That is for discharge subsequently to some date in September. I forget the date upon which the order in council was passed.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: .She is entitled to it from the date in September, I believe it was, when the order in council was passed, but she would not get it for the period from May to September.
To whom would wives make application in England or Scotland for that allowance, if they were not receiving it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: They should not have to make application. But if they are not receiving it they should apply to the Canadian wives bureau in London, and elsewhere. But from the records here the cheque should go forward automatically.
There is no wives bureau in Scotland; it is just in England is it?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Just in London.
Is it contemplated to date it back earlier than September?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: No.
That will not be done?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: No.
Is that the ordinary dependents' allowance?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The regular dependents' allowance, yes.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Travel, transportation and freight, $65,939,968.
Demobilization-Army
What priorities are given to wives of ex-servicemen in connection with transportation from Great Britain to Canada? There are priorities; what are they?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Well, priorities are pretty low at the present, tifaie. We are not bringing very many of them back. But the hon. member meant, no doubt, in what way would priorities be given as between applicants'in Great Britain and others?
Yes.
