speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I am advised there are five orders of priority. The first, of course, is for compassionate cases. I believe the next is where the husband is discharged. But before giving a complete answer I had better get the order of priority. I have not that information with me.
Practically all the husbands of these wives have been discharged.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Not necessarily.
But. there are a great many. I wonder what priority they have?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: In that case the priority would be the date on which she makes her application to the Canadian wives bureau.
Do officers' wives have any priority?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: No.
I ask that in order to clear up what I consider to be a misunderstanding.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: They have no priority.
That is all I wanted to know.

Following the question
asked by the hon. member for Peterborough West, I realize that this may not be a popular question, but it is an important one. There are a great many soldiers' wives overseas and there is considerable hardship, not only for those wives who are overseas but for wives who have returned to Canada. In the case of wives on this side, the husbands are on the other side; in the case of wives in England, the husbands are here. It. would seem to me that the department could do something without affecting the return of the soldiers themselves. I know the minister takes the attitude that his department has the responsibility of seeing that the men get back, and that is correct. However, I do not think it would affect the return of the soldiers very much if he tried to make some special arrangements to have the wives returned, perhaps at the same time as their husbands. There are quite a numbei* of ships bringing

men back to Canada, and I suggest that the minister could take possibly one of the smaller ships and set it aside to bring back the wives and husbands at the same time. These men have to set up housekeeping and establish their homes in Canada. Many of the wives who have come back are living with their in-laws and others. I know from letters I get from the Red Cross, the I.O.D.E. and other women's organizations that there is considerable hardship in this connection.
Will the minister give consideration to an attempt to relieve the situation and bring back these wives and their husbands as close together as possible? This should be part of our reestablishment programme and we should give it serious consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
We are giving it consideration. It is a most difficult problem, as the committee will appreciate. I do not want to make any public announcement and hold out any false hopes. It may be that with additions to our shipping-some smaller ships as my hon. friend suggests-we shall be able to bring back more wives and dependents than we are able to do at the moment. I do not know that it would be desirable to bring the wives and the husbands back in the same vessel. We have had the troopships fitted out with a large number of bunks to a cabin, and we can bring back men under conditions under which women and children could not very well be carried. I think in the interests of efficiency and economy it would be better to bring back the wives and dependents-small children require special diet and so on-in ships fitted up for that purpose.
I do not wish to hold out false hopes, but I want to assure the committee, the people of the country and those who are interested in this problem, the men who are waiting for their wives to come out, that every consideration is being given and every effort being made to bring them back as soon as we can. Speaking generally, where there is still a shortage of shipping, I still feel that the men who have been away from their wives in Canada for a long time should have first priority.
While I am discussing this question of wives I should like to correct some figures that I gave with respect to the number of wives and dependents who have been returned. The figures had been given to me and I was perhaps a little optimistic. I said that the total of the services that had been returned to date was approximately 20,000. I am sorry to say that it is not quite as large as that. The total of army wives and children is 11,890, and I think the figures for the other two services would run to something like another, 4,000. The total is something over 15,000. There is

Demobilization-Army
a question on the order paper and I shall give the exact figure. I was about 4,000 out in my total when I gave it the other day.

How many are still in
the old country?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
There are about 21,017 wives and 8,273 children, according to the last report, but I think those figures are still increasing. I will give the order of repatriation of wives which my hon. friend asked for a moment ago. It is as follows:
Husband discharged from service.
Husband in hospital in Canada.
Dependent pregnant.	_
Husband repatriated ex-prisoner of war.
Husband repatriated to Canada and still in service.
Compassionate eases including widows.
Normal repatriation.

I wish to associate myself with what the hon. member for Royal has said and also to ask the minister a brief question. Is he aware that the Canadian wives bureau in England has been assuring the wives of soldiers who have been returned that to all intents and purposes they would be on the way themselves within thirty days? That information has been given to me quite recently by members of the armed forces who have been returned but whose wives are still in the old country.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It is clearly unauthorized and I doubt very much if it was given by anyone in the wives bureau. I had hoped that the statement I made some time ago would have been given fairly wide publicity. I know it resulted in a delegation of husbands coming from Toronto to see me. In any event any such information is completely unauthorized.

There is one other point I wish to clear up. The minister intimated to me privately that no wives were being brought to this country, except on extremely compassionate grounds, whose husbands are still in the army of occupation or in other services in Europe. If people tell me that that is so, shall I be correct in trying to convince them that they are wrong?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes.

I wanted to make sure because I have two more letters on that point. I am not trying to make it difficult for the minister; I simply want to be able to tell these people exactly what is being done. It may be just rumours that they have heard.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It is only a rumour. But I shall be glad to have the names.

Does this item for travel, transportation and freight cover the transportation back to Canada of the wives and1 children of all the armed services, or do the other two services and perhaps the Department of Immigration bear a share of the cost? Also who pays the cost of the Canadian wives bureau? I was subjected to a conducted tour through the Canadian wives bureau last January, and personally I thought it was the most overstaffed branch of C.M.H.Q. Every department of C.M.H.Q. is tremendously- overstaffed.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The cost of transportation of all wives from whatever service is charged to the army vote. We are responsible for repatriating the dependents of all three services. The cost of the Canadian wives bureau is also charged to this vote, but whether it comes under this item, I am not sure.

I have been trying to study these figures which the minister has presented to the committee and, while I believe that the minister is asking for more money than he should have voted to him in many cases, here is one case in which I believe his departmental officials must have underestimated the amount that will ibe required. During 1944-45 $60,490,401 was spent under this item, and the estimate for 1915-46 is $65,939,968. It seems to me that with the tremendous increase in the number of our troops being returned to Canada, the amount required for this year should be much greater than it was last year, and an explanation is due from the minister in that regard. He should also tell us the cost of the transportation of troops from Europe, to England and from England to Canada, say to Halifax or Montreal, so that we may have some idea of the number of troops that will be included in this estimate.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
The decrease of $27,000,000 odd is attributable to three factors. First, a capitation rate has been set for the transportation of all personnel, vehicles and stores in continental Europe and the United Kingdom, with a considerable reduction in cost from last year's estimate. . These matters are handled on a capitation basis. Second, vehicle and personnel shipments overseas are greatly reduced. Third, there are no initial charges for hospital ships. The cost of railway transportation in Canada for personnel proceeding to embarkation points and other repatriates returning to the home depot have been shifted to activity No. 1, with which I shall deal in a moment. That accounts in part for the reduction in expenditure in activity No. 2.
Before describing the two branches, I might outline what this item provides for. It- provides for all expenses incurred in connection with the movement of personnel, supplies and

Demobilization-Army
equipment, and the costs are set out under two heads. The first includes travel and transportation in the United Kingdom, Europe and the United States. Second, ocean transportation and freight, Canada to the United Kingdom, and the reverse. Third, railway transportation of repatriates from disembarkation point to home depot or hospital. Next, railway transportation to embarkation point of reinforcements and personnel returning to Europe from rotation leave in Canada. Next, railway freight from depot or factory to take on vehicles shipped overseas, and finally railway and ocean freight on stores and equipment returned from the United' Kingdom to Canada.
Activity No. 2 I need not review in detail. It covers transportation items in Canada. Activity No. 3 covers miscellaneous transportation costs for the reserve army, but mainly transportation to the annual training camps.	-
Under activity No. 1, that is the overseas disbursements, the estimates this year are $44,475,737, or a-reduction of $23,374,514.
Under activity No. 2, that is the Canadian end, the total is $20,318,453, which includes a carryover of some two million dollars from the previous fiscal period. That represents a reduction of $2,943,226.
For the third category, that is the reserve army in annual training camps and for miscellaneous transportation costs, the estimate is $1,145,778, or a reduction of $700,158. The over-all reduction in the estimates is $27,017,898.

Once again I would draw the minister's attention to the actual expenditures. I do not think it is right for the minister to give the committee just the estimates. I think we should know what the actual expenditures were.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: They have been given.

The expenditures for 1944-45 were $60,000,000 odd and the minister is asking for 1945-46 S65,000,000 odd. I asked the minister to inform the committee what the transportation costs were for the individual crossing the Atlantic.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: For activity No. 1, which includes personnel, equipment and so on, the per capita rate last year was $66.75 for an adult.
Both east and west?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Either way. For children over five and under twelve, fifty per cent of

the adult rate; for children over one and under five, twenty-five per cent of the adult rate; for children under one year, $3.35.
I want a comparison of the actual expenditures.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Perhaps that could be
obtained.
It does not matter'on this item, but I would like the minister to give it on future items.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It would be easy to get that. Of course it is pretty hard to foresee just how members of the committee will want the break-down presented. If we cannot get it before we finish with these estimates I will undertake to bring this information down with information that was to be given on the navy estimates and answer a number of queries at the same time, possibly to-morrow or when the committee next sits.
What I am trying to get is a comparison of the actual expenditures of last year with the estimates for the present year, I think the minister could make some kind of comparison.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The expenditures for 194445 were $60,490,401 and the estimates for 1945-46 are $65,939,968, but my hon. friend, I understand, wants the actual expenditures for 1944-45 further broken down.
Yes, for other items. It does not matter about this item.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I have had distributed
among the members a sheet showing the army estimates and expenditures for 1944-45 and the estimates for 1945-46.
I have that. But what I was interested in was the actual expenditures, to compare them with the estimates.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: We can break down the expenditures under the same three heads. But the estimate book -which I have before me deals with this year's estimates, not last. The figures are readily available. Every one of these actual expenditures for 1944-45 can probably be broken down in the same way as the estimates are broken down here. But the estimate book which I had in giving this information has never been prepared in that way. We give the totals, and then, if any member of the committee is interested in any particular item, the break-down has always been made readily available. In some, the committee may not be interested.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Perhaps the committee
need not take much more time on this matter in order to have clearly understood the point

Demobilization-Army
that the hon. member for York South was trying to make. The minister in explaining these items compared, the estimates for this year with the estimates for last year. What the hon. member for York South wants is a comparison of the estimates of this year with the actual expenditures for last year.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That has been given.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
But in the minister's
explanation he did not give what the hon. member wanted. He tied his explanation of this year's estimates to the estimates for last year rather than to the expenditures of last year. I do not think there is any misunderstanding of what he wants. If we compare the estimates of this year with the estimates of last year, look what we get. The estimates of this year compared with the estimates, for last year are $27 million less, but the estimates of this year compared with the expenditures of last year are $5 million more. The only point the hon. member for York South was trying to make was that if the minister will compare the estimates of this year with the actual expenditures of last year the figures will mean something, while comparing this year's estimates with the estimates of last year means little or nothing.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: In some cases they are up; in some eases they are down. As I have explained so often before, particularly with respect to war expenditures, estimating is a very difficult task. You cannot tell how many vehicles will be used. It is hard to tell how much your pay and allowances will be. Your estimates vary a great deal. I used a very unfortunate phrase in the navy estimates, which I am not going to repeat because it got me into hot water. But my hon. friend is quite right, that it is probably more useful to compare estimates with actual expenditures, and it was for that reason I had these sheets prepared for distribution, showing the three items of last year's estimates, last year's actual, and this year's estimates; and the second sheet was added to give the operating results for the first six months of this year, to indicate h-ow this year's estimates were working out.

I should like to know
whether a soldier on compassionate leave who is called to report at the nearest military district for his discharge is entitled to refund of his fare if, on arrival at the military district, he is told that a mistake has been made and that he is to return home to continue on compassionate leave.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Cases of that kind have
to be looked into individually. Certain cases
of that kind have come to my attention and refunds have been made. But each case has to be considered on its merits.

I should like the minister
to explain how the expenditure is proportioned between the three services in respect of transportation from overseas. When the boats come back from the old country they have on board airmen, navy men and army men. How is the expense allocated to the three different services?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
The army pays them, and
then the other two services for accounting purposes are charged on the capitation rate that I mentioned.
A per capita basis?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
That is right-on a per
capita. That is the way we settle for our transportation overseas. We have an arrangement with the British which is based on a capitation rate. It has been worked out over the period of the war and I think in some cases was finally settled only during the last few months.
Which department arranges for the chartering of the ships?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The army.

I should like to ask the minister regarding the use of Camp Borden, Barrie has been known for some time as a military town. The merchants there rely a good deal on the money spent by soldiers residing at Camp Borden. There will no doubt be a reduction in the personnel of soldiers and air force men at Camp Borden, and the purchasing power of these men will be greatly missed by the merchants of Barrie. There is and has been for years an establishment at Stanley barracks of the permanent force with, I believe, inadequate, grounds for proper training. Would the minister bear in mind, when cutting expense and increasing efficiency in the army, that the vacant barracks should be used at Camp Borden by the permanent soldiers * from Stanley, by the removal of these soldiers from the Stanley barracks, from a large centre such as Toronto, to provide great benefits to a small community like Barrie, Ontario? I would ask the minister to consider that in the interest of the reduction of costs and the increase of efficiency of the army.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
May I point out that we are on item 3, travel, transportation and freight. I do not see how the statement made by the hon. member for Simcoe North comes
Demobilization-Army

within that item, and I wonder whether we could leave the discussion of it until we come to the item in which it is included.

One matter in connection with the repatriation. There has been strong criticism of the fact that in a recent voyage of the Queen Elizabeth five per cent of those on board were civilians. The criticism is that a number of civilians, unnecessary in Canada, travelled on that ship. I have received letters from men overseas who complain about that. They point out that 600 civilians, not including wives and dependents of soldiers, are altogether too great a number of civilians to be permitted to travel on ships designated for the return of servicemen. Is the minister in a position to answer that question?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes, I can answer that. The Queen Elizabeth, as well as other boats, has been obtained from the British ministry of shipping, and it is obtained on condition that a certain limited amount of space is reserved for civilian passengers engaged in necessary travel. Members of the committee will realize that certain civilians have to travel. We have no control over those who oecupy that limited amount of space. That must be obtained from the British ministry of shipping.
Did the minister in an earlier statement to-night say that we have a special ship equipped to carry from England to this country the wives of our Canadian servicemen?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Not yet.
May I ask if we intend to have one?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: We hope we may have.
If we have one, will it be under the control of the Canadian army?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Construction, purchase, repairs and operating expenses of properties: (a) capital expenditure. $11,031,465; (b) repairs, operating expenses and rentals, $29,745,798.

I take it that this is the item to which the remark of the hon. member for Simcoe North pertained. I have not heard any intimation that there was a thought on the part of the minister to close up Stanley barracks in Toronto.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I have not heard of it myself.

I trust there is no thought of removing the permanent force unit, which Toronto has been glad to accommodate, from that great city.	.
[The Chairman.]

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: No decision in the matter has yet been made.

My suggestion was made purely to save the country an immense sum of money. It was not that I wanted to derive any benefit that Toronto may be receiving. In order to save the public's money and to benefit the army generally I made the suggestion to the minister to move the force from Stanley barracks to the town of Barrie.

The minister has intimated that there will be a permanent force of from twenty to twenty-five thousand men. It is hoped that the permanent force will^be modern in every sense of the word. In order to attract the right sort of young men into the permanent force it is essential that they be housed in up-to-date and modern buildings. I do not care where they are, anywhere across the dominion. For the past twenty years there have been very few permanent barracks constructed. There was a small barracks constructed outside Calgary, the Currie barracks, and the Vimy Ridge barracks constructed near Kingston. During the war a large number of camps were built, but the huts in those camps are of an essentially temporary nature. There have been very few, if any, permanent barracks constructed. I realize that the bulk of that construction will no doubt be carried out under the Department of Public Works, but it is essential, if we are to have a first-class regular or active army, or whatever it is called, that the personnel be housed in up-to-date barracks. I see no indication here that adequate funds are being provided for the maintenance of such buildings. Could the minister give some idea of what construction work is planned in connection with the future force?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: A plan has been prepared for the sort of thing to which my hon. friend has been referring, and it has been referred to the Department of Reconstruction, the idea being, of course, that the time at which projects of that kind should be initiated should be decided by the Department of Reconstruction. Our plans have been prepared and turned .over to the Department of Reconstruction for decision by that department as to when and if the work should be gone ahead with.
If we are going to recruit that force now we must have some place to put them in.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Quite.

Temporary buildings are of a very poor nature. If the construction

D emobilization-Army
programme is not going to come off for perhaps a number of years there will be difficulty in holding that force.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I appreciate that, but I think the committee will realize that other forms of ouilding are a little more urgent just at the moment, including housing, to which refer-3nce was made.
Does this item refer to buildings or rentals in Britain?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Included in the item is an amount of approximately 89,667,000, which represents the capitation rate for the accommodation of our army overseas. It is between ten pence and eleven pence a day. That, as well as feeding and other charges, is settled on the basis of a capitation rate, so much per man. The British provide the accommodation, pay whatever rental there is, and so on, and we pay them the capitation rate for it.
Does that include officers?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services

speechtext: I should like to ask the minister a question in connection with that particular item of new construction, $2,424,546. His officials would be able to advise him that for many years plans were under consideration for a new military headquarters in M.D. No. 6. Included in that new military headquarters was an extension through a street known as Brunswick street. The idea was to transfer a certain portion from the department of defence to the city of Halifax, and to erect a new military headquarters on a new site. Is this $2,424,546, the item that has been set aside for this particular work?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I am advised that there is
no large single item of construction included in the figure I have mentioned. It includes a large variety of comparatively small projects. I think the one to which my hon. friend has referred must be held over for a subsequent year.
May we be given some more particulars about the construction? What construction has been done?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I have a mass of detail
here. I find there is an item of a fairly substantial amount included here for Halifax, new Wellington barracks for Royal Canadian Army Service Corps, motor transport garage, and so on. There is an item here of some $210,000.

I thank the minister; I
thought there must be something there.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
That is subject, of course,
to the approval of the Department of Reconstruction in the same way as the others to which I referred. We put it in the estimates; what will happen to it I do not know.

What construction has been
done this year? Where has it been done? AVho did it, and what did it cost in each instance? What further construction is to be done this year; where will it be done, and what is the estimated cost? What properties were purchased this year; where were they located; from whom were they purchased; what was paid for them? Is it the intention to purchase any further properties this year? If so, where are those properties located, and what is the estimated price? Perhaps the minister cannot answer all these questions just now.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
My hon. friend asked
similar questions when the navy estimates were before the committee. I almost felt like asking the chairman if he had made them an order for return. The information will be available; I shall get it and furnish it as soon as possible. '

I have two questions I should like to ask. They refer to the boys training school at Bowmanville. I believe there was an agreement entered into by the government of Ontario and the dominion government in connection with it. As a result this school was turned over in 1941 for use as a prison camp for German officers. I understand1 it was to be returned to the province and restored for use as a boys training school just as soon as there was mo further need for it as a prison camp. I believe 'the German prisoners were moved in April, and I am wondering if anything is being done to restore this property.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes, it is all being taken care of. I believe the Department of Munitions and Supply has let the contract to put the school back in shape, and that work is now under way.
Could the minister say whether the work has started as yet?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I could not be sure as to that, but I will inquire and find out. If not, it will start very shortly.

Demobilization-Army

Is anything being done or will anything be done in regard to building a new armouries in Port Hope? The old armouries there were condemned years agio, and all we have at the present time is an old church building, which has been used as m armouries all during the war.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I shall have to give my hon. friend the answer I have given a number of others who have asked the same question. This is a matter for consideration by the Department of Reconstruction. Projects of that kind are decided upon by that department.

I notice that the estimate for this year is $40,776,000, while the amount expended last year was $43,000,000, so that there is a reduction of only $3,000,000. The expenditure so far this year has been $12,500,000. Is it expected that the amount to be expended this year will be very much reduced below the estimate of $40,000,000? Has any further estimate been made in that connection?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Any reduction will depend largely upon whether or not we do any new construction. As I showed in the break-down I gave, the estimates include some considerable 'amount for new construction. Whether or not that is proceeded with will depend upon the decision taken by the Department of Reconstruction. Any substantial reduction would result from failure to proceed with the construction programme which has been provided for in the estimates.
I suppose it is istimated that this amount of $29,700,000 will be materially reduced as time goes on; that is in connection with rentals and repairs?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes. Actually, of course, operating expenses for the first six months have amounted to twenty-eight per cent of the estimates. If that ratio should be maintained in the latter half of the year the estimates would be cut substantially. It is hard to say just how it will work out in the end, but we have the operating results for six months now.
How many arsenals have we under the control of the Department of National Defence, and where are they located?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
At the moment there are none under the Department of National Defence. During the war they were all administered by the Department of Munitions and Supply, and that condition still exists. That

question came up in connection with another matter, I believe under the navy estimates, and I suggested to the hon. member who asked it that probably more detailed and accurate information could be obtained when the Minister of Munitions and Supply takes up his estimates.

I have a further question that I suppose I might better ask a little later, but I think it has direct reference to this matter. What plan has the Department of National Defence adopted to ensure that Canada may continue to manufacture up-to-date munitions of war for the new army? The minister quite rightly said that our army, navy and air force would be provided with the very latest equipment. Is it proposed that we shall ourselves equip those forces, or is it proposed that we shall buy the material somewhere else?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: At the moment we have on hand quite a lot of the material and equipment. In future I think we will both manufacture and probably have to buy. As to the details, again I suggest that my hon. friend would get a more satisfactory answer if he addressed that question to the Minister of Munitions and Supply, who has been in charge of planning our armament production throughout the war.

In that connection I have a vivid recollection of what occurred in Canada a few years ago, when it was not understood just what arsenals were. I think a great deal of credit should be given the former director of the national research council, General McNaughton, for his foresight in the early days of the depression, when he had the vision to encourage the establishment of pilot plants for the development of the art of manufacturing munitions of war. Such pilot plants were set up by the national research council, and during the war we greatly benefited from those plants and from the research that was carried on. I mention as an example the development of magnesium; the construction of the wind tunnel; the research carried on in connection with boats, and so on. To my way of thinking we should not forget the lesson we learned in the early days of this war. If we had maintained well equipped arsenals in this country; if we had established liaison with Great Britain and the United States, and so on, I think we would have been far better equipped to manufacture our own munitions of war. We would have had trained workmen; we would have had the art of manufacturing these things. I might mention a very good example. Without detracting at all from what was done by the

Demobilization-Army
John Inglis company in connection with 'tfhe manufacture of Bren guns, I have it on good authority that thousands of dollars could have been saved in the early days if the manufacture of that gun had been undertaken in a small pilot plant at an early date, instead of trying to develop the art in a great factoiy. We all know the number of rejects that came through in that factory for months.
I am bringing up these matters only to show how necessary it is for the Department of National Defence to have close liaison, through the Department of Reconstruction or the Department of Munitions and Supply, with the manufacturers of the country, so that we shall not lose the benefits of what we have learned in connection with the manufacture of these things. It seems to me that we should continue to have pilot plants operating and also that, even if it costs a little more, the Department of National Defence should buy whatever it requires from Canadian manufacturers. One part of research on which we should keep up to date all the time is that having to do with the manufacture of these munitions of war.

I should like to ask the minister one other question in connection with certain properties in the city of Halifax taken over by the Department of National Defence. I am sure I do not need to emphasize readiness and willingness with which the people of Halifax placed at the disposal of the department the exhibition grounds, where the navy was first quartered, and where there is now a barracks, the new Wellington barracks. Then there is the other property, known as Che-bucto barracks, or No. 6 district depot, which was formerly the Halifax airport. The city is very anxious to know when that property will be available for its use, so that I would ask the minister if he is in a position to advise as to how soon his department will be able to return that property to the city of Halifax.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I an afraid I cannot give my hon. friend any exact date, except to say that we are trying to get out of all exhibition properties as soon as possible. We realize that there is a natural desire on the part of local communities to have those properties available for exhibition purposes. However, I cannot give any exact date. '

Perhaps I did not make myself clear. I am not greatly concerned about the exhibition. But the exhibition property lends itself in a fundamental way to future development. I hope the minister will see his way clear to segregate army troops in that particular section of Halifax, where they should
have been some years ago. In fact, I think he will find on record in his office plans which would take in that policy. I am not at this time advocating the return 'of the exhibition grounds, but I am interested in the return of the property known as No. 6 district depot, or the Halifax airport property.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I shall have to make inquiries. We are trying to get out of properties of that kind as quickly as we can.

Many questions are being
asked of the minister, and perhaps I might assist him by making a suggestion. I notice that in this item only thirty-one per cent of the appropriation was spent in the first six months. It would seem, therefore, that the department will end up with a surplus. I would take a leaf out of the book of the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Ferguson) and suggest to the minister that if he would like to build a barracks where it will be greatly appreciated he might just speak to me privately, and I would tell him where to locate it.	.

Apropos of what
I said in connection with liaison between the Department of National Defence and other departments, what is to be the policy in that connection?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: In connection with arsenals and research work?
Yes, in connection with having these things made in the country, and keeping up to date, and not losing the benefit of what we have done in the' war.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Perhaps the hon. member
was not in his seat when I replied to a question asked by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes). I said that the plan for research and development contemplates close liaison between industry and the defence services of the country. The method to be followed 1 is now under study, and I am not in a position to make any positive statement as to what that method will be. I can, however, assure the committee that this matter is not being overlooked, and that it is being given the most careful and anxious consideration at this time.

I should like to ask the minister two, questions, the first of which has to do with the Alaska highway. Last week the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) in his capacity as acting Secretary of State for External Affairs explained to the house that the Canadian army was to take over the maintenance of the Alaska highway.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
As of April 1, yes.
Demobilization-Army
Yes, as of April 1, 1946. That, I believe, will be a new job for the Canadian army?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes; that is right.

I have no doubt there will
be a good many problems to settle. Is the minister in a position to give us any information on the point this evening? For example, can he tell us whether it will be under the supervision of the Royal Canadian Engineers or just what the plan will be?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I can reply in a general
way. As a matter of fact, the Canadian army was keenly interested in taking over the maintenance of the Alaska highway, because it will afford an opportunity for practical training in bridge construction, and that sort of thing by the engineering corps. It is felt that that will be of interest to the younger men coming in. For this reason the army is interested- in taking over the highway. We take over as of April 1, so that there is no provision in this year's estimates. Next year, however, there will have to be an estimate to make provision for the maintenance and upkeep of the Alaska highway. The staff is now giving this matter careful consideration, in consultation with United States military authorities who have been in charge up to the present time, and who have made available their cost figures to show what provision we shall have to make.

My second question has to
do with the possibility of the army's giving up some of the building space it now occupies. I would imagine that -the situation is much the same in every province of Canada. However, in Vancouver the army took over the old Vancouver hotel which, as the minister is no doubt aware, is a very large building. Some suggestion was made a few weeks ago that the army was to clear out, and have someone take over the building. However, no definite announcement has been made.
It is of the utmost importance that there be some reduction in space occupied by government departments. For example. I have letters from doctors who are returning from overseas, after having served for several years;
I receive letters from lawyers and from other men who require office- space, and all tell me that they are having the utmost difficulty in finding any space at all. If the army could cut down on the space being used it would be helpful in reestablishing these men.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I can assure my hon. friend that this question is receiving daily consideration, not only by the officers of the department,

but by myself. I am sure there is not a morning conference goes by when, in meeting with the staff, we do not have some, question before us in which a request has been made to vacate some space. We are doing our best to meet these requests.
The committee will realize that we still have a fairly heavy problem on our hands, with demobilization, the storage of equipment and the like, with the result that it is not possible to move out as rapidly as we might wish. However, we are making shifts from property which may be used for purposes such as have been suggested by the hon. member, and moving into other types of property situated perhaps in more remote areas. AVe can do that now. He is right when he says that this is an important point, and I can assure him that we are doing the best we can to see that the necessary changes are made.
What about the old Vancouver hotel?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is under-to use a popular expression-the most active consideration at the present time. I am -not in a position yet to make a positive statement on the point, but I hope before long I may be able to do so.
May I revert to the Alaska highway, because I know something about the road, having been over it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: May I point out that it is not covered by this item.
Is the minister in a position to tell the committee if the engineering department has made any estimate as to the cost of taking care of the Alaska highway?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Not yet. That will have to be included in next year's estimates. We are now conferring with United States authorities who have had under their control the upkeep of that highway, to find out what their costs have been. We are preparing estimates, but I cannot give any statement at this time.

I might say that I conferred with the United States engineers on the highway in connection with keeping it in order after the war was over. The information I got was that for the first year it would cost approximately $15 million, but that from then on it would cost approximately $5 million a year.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
The information I have is that the highway is in good condition to-day. I should have thought the hon. member's figure is pretty high.

Demobilization-Army
Does the minister mean my figure of $5 million?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I thought the hon. member said $15 million.
I gave .that amount for the first year.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I would not be in a position to give any figure. I have no doubt my hon. friend's information is pretty good.

-All the non-permanent bridges would probably have to be rebuilt the first year. However, quite a number are permanent and they should not have to be rebuilt. I am of opinion that perhaps they were right in stating that the yearly cost would be about $5 million, once we have it in shape.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Personnel supplies and services; food, medical and dental stores, clothing and personal equipment, $142,857,171.

The actual expenditures on this item in the fiscal year 1944-45 were $153,569,439. I notice that the estimate for 1945-46 is $142,857,171, or a reduction of about $11 million. The war was over in May, so far as the European war is concerned. But it does seem to me there should be a greater reduction in this amount than is shown here, for the simple reason that the minister has told the committee that, up to date, 100,000 men have been demobilized, and this item includes personnel supplies, food, medical and dental stores. There must certainly be an explanation for a figure which is so much out of line as this one is.

Before 'the minister gives
his answer, I wish to say a few things about clothing and personal equipment. This amount is quite large. I should like to know what is done with military clothing which has been worn and which is returned to the department. I understand that some of this clothing is given to the soldier, but that what is left is given to the Indians or sold by the pound. During the war a colonization agent in my constituency tried to buy some of this clothing for settlers and settlers' children. He was told to wait until after the war. Now this clothing is in the hands of War Assets Corporation.
An hon MEMBER:	Or destroyed.

Or burned or sold to the
man who makes a huge profit from dealing in that kind of clothing. The acting leader of the house must remember the days when he was the Minister of National Defence. I was proud of him because he did veTy well. He has a quality which the two
ministers before the present minister did not have; he is human. He understood the difficulties faced by people, as did Norman Rogers and as does the present incumbent of this post. But the others did not.
I remember the time when General LaFleche was deputy to the minister. I told him of the _ difficulties faced by settlers whose children had to stay indoors all winter without going out to play in the snow because they had no clothing. The kind heart of the minister did not have to mellow because he had a good heart. He understood the problem of these people, and he decided to distribute some of this clothing which was no longer of use to the army to relieve the distress of the poor and to give an opportunity to these young children to have some warm clothing in the winter. The minister probably has forgotten his good actions on that occasion, but I remember them and those whose suffering was relieved by his ffindness still remember that. They have to have good memories because since then they have got nothing. What happened? The war expenditures committee acted foolishly and listened to some brass hate who had no heart and who suggested that everything should be sold to the junk dealer. I do not know if they were agents of the junk dealers, or if tl^ey had a share in the benefits from the sale of those goods. It may have happened because it does happen sometimes. I was scandalized to see those men with hearts of- stone refuse to give a chance to the poor of this country.
They were ready to give this clothing to the Indians, which is all right for the Indians. The hon. member for Calgary East has suggested that the Indians should have the same rights as the whites as far as old age pensions are concerned. That is quite fair, but I think the least we should expect is that the whites should have the same rights as the Indians. When there is poverty in our midst it is the duty of men in public life to realize that family allowances are not enough * to cover expenditures incurred by parents when bringing up a large family. When there is an opportunity to provide some generous help, they should not miss that opportunity. These people are poor, but they are proud. They sometimes resent the way in which charity is offered, but something given by the state is not charity that brings humiliation to their hearts. They accept willingly their share of what belongs to the country. What belongs to the country, belongs to the people at large. It belongs to all the people, but it should be distributed to those who need it most.
Demobilization-Army

I do not see why anyone should have to pay anything for a wise and judicious distribution of this clothing to the needy, to those among us who are suffering. We hear a lot about public health. There is a committee of the house of which I am a member, but I must say that I have not attended any sitting. I am not interested because it is mainly academic. I am not interested in academic matters; I am interested in facts and actions. If a thing is not done according to scientific formulae the experts of the Department of Health and Welfare will turn it down, even though it achieves its aim. They have fine brains, but they are brains that should be kept under glass in a coffin to be exposed to all passers by. Their brains are so large that they take up all the space in their bodies and no room is left for a heart. That is how health and welfare is understood in Ottawa. Do you think that cheques will cure all the evil? Cheques are good and cheques are appreciated, but cheques of $5 or $6 or $7 will not buy all the warm clothing that the young ones need, especially in the winter that is coming very quickly. I know that the minister will tell me: You will have to put your request before War Assets Corporation. But there is not time. The minister is piloting this estimate-
He is not piloting; he is anchored.
My hon. frie#nd will pardon me if I use a nautical expression in reference to the ship of state.
That is clever.

But here we are. Let us give our imaginations an opportunity to picture the huge quantities of clothing and personal equipment amounting to $159,000,000 worth. That is a very large bouquet on the desk of the minister, to purchase new clothing and personal equipment.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That was last year's estimate. It is $142,000,000 this year,

It makes little difference when we are dealing with such big figures. If it were only $100,000,000, it would be something. It is a formidable sum of money, perhaps not formidable to the government but certainly formidable to me. This money is to buy new clothes and new equipment, and perhaps there will be certain services and supplies. It is a very large amount, to purchase a very' large quantity of new clothing to replace another large quantity of clothing which is not so good, naturally, as the new clothing but which still may be quite service-
able to mothers who would tailor it into good warm clothing for their young children. Here I must pay a special tribute to the Canadian mother, who is just as industrious as a bee, and who takes advantage of her natural skill to do things that would seem to man to be impossible. Is it not possible to bring this matter to the attention not only of the minister but of the whole cabinet? It would bring relief to a large number of families, and would cost the government nothing, except the small amount that would otherwise be got from the junk dealers. The cost is nothing compared with the good that would come to the nation if the government would act as it has done in distant past years. I know the minister is well disposed on many matters, and I hope that he will speak to the Minister of Reconstruction, under whose administration War Assets Corporation comes, so that some of this clothing may be widely distributed to the needy through charitable organizations, the Red Cross, parish priests and municipal councils. It would be a good act and it would help the families of the settlers as much as family allowance.
While I am on my feet I wish to pay a special tribute to the very finest man who was in the Department of National Defence during the past year, Colonel Henri Des-Rosiers, who has won many decorations and who led the famous 22nd battalion into Germany after the last war. I have been told by my friends and my relatives what a gallant officer he was then. After the war he occupied the high position of vice-president of the Imperial Tobacco company in Montreal. He left that position to come to Ottawa to fulfil a most ungrateful task. I had to write to him again and again, and "if there was no revolution in my county it was due to the fairness and spirit of justice and to the really manly qualities of Colonel DesRosiers. I owe him a special tribute. He has helped the poor by very fine acts of charity, and he has helped some soldiers, who did not know a word of English and who had only Englishspeaking officers, to get transferred to other positions. He has also been a wise adviser to the ministers of national defence who unfortunately did not ask often enough for hia advice. He was the ideal man in the pfiblic service. He worked in team with the present incumbent of the office of deputy minister. Colonel DesRosiers has not been replaced, and the fact that he has not been replaced in the position of deputy minister is a great loss to French Canadians, and not only French Canadians but to all who are French speaking. There is a reason for that. As we have the same expenditures practically

D e mobilization-A rm y
in the Department of National Defence as during the war there must be the same amount of work to be done as there was before, and as there were two deputy ministers during the war I do not see how one can fulfil all the tasks now. The estimates are nearly as big this year as last. There are good men among the French-speaking officers in the army, but they have not an opportunity to serve in the Department of National Defence.
Replying to what was said by one of the new members, we might take, for instance, Major-General Tremblay, one of the finest men in the army. He also was commander of the 22nd regiment. His chest is full of decorations which he won on the battlefield. He has a fine reputation not only in Canada but overseas as well, and plenty of friends. He was appointed inspector-general of the army in the eastern command. What did he do? For months and months, perhaps for more than a year, or even two years, he was seconded by the Department of National Defence to the Department of Labour to act as a buffer in matters of man-power. He was there as a clerk and tool of Ralston, while there was no inspector-general to look after these needs of the army in the eastern command. He kept his position as inspector-general but he could not fill it. This is only one example, but the time is late, and I will not quote any more. This sort of thing shows that when competent men are assigned to a certain duty in the army they are removed to be clerks-minor clerks-in other departments where their work is not as useful as it would have been had they been left at their original posts. I could tell much more, but that, I think, is enough for the present.
I want my compatriots from the province of Quebec to be respected; and if there are no more who have important positions it is because they are kept in the dark by those who are interested in not bringing them into the limelight and who may be jealous of them.
The minister is fair-minded; he is living in the big city of Montreal; he knows that some of his best friends are French Canadians and the value of those who are French Canadians. I was touched when I listened to the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard say that he had met French-Canadian officers when he was in German concentration camps, and there he knew them and was able to judge the quality of the province of Quebec by the character of her sons.
We hope that the minister will do, what has not been done by Colonel Ralston or General McNaughton, namely, bring reform into the 47696-111
Department of National Defence. It is a very hard task, and Mr. Chairman, I will tell you why. It is because of the men of the department who are around a minister. I do not speak particularly of the Minister of National Defence; it applies to all departments. These people have meals together; sometimes their wives are friendly. If this or that man is fired they will complain to the minister and say, "Oh, So-and-so, why did you do that to him?" Wives like to talk to each other; then there will be trouble in the house, and friends will come there and say-I do not speak of any minister in particular-"Why did you do that to your friend? You were unjust." Then the chiefs of the branches have their own friends; they are friendly with the deputy; their wives meet and have parties together; they form a sort of family compact which it is hard to destroy. People may suffer on account of the incompetence of individuals, but there is close friendship between some of them, and it is impossible to break those links, to cut those ties and >
say, "You, So-and-so are incompetent; it is unfortunate, but you will have to go and make room for a competent one." It is a hard thing to do. Things like that go on all the time, and that is why we have no reform. It takes more courage to bring reform into the Department of National Defence or any other department than to fight a war against any enemy, because reform of this kind has to be done in peace time, when the world is supposed to be full of men of good will, and as all men are supposed to be full of good will, how can we call anyone incompetent? The one who calls him incompetent is not supposed to have any good will; the other is regarded as a victim; and so we cannot have reform.
However, it is nearly eleven o'clock. Some hon. members may have something important to say. I hope the ministers will not forget, even in their sleep, what I have said, and if they decide to bring reform they will deserve and receive fine treatment.
